newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: WEEK AHEAD-Australia markets wary of Dow slump.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-Australia markets wary of Dow slump.

text.p: Wall Street's second largest points slump ever on Friday night is expected to set the tone for Australia's stock market early this week, but a similar slump is seen unlikely here because many were sceptical of the rally that preceded the slump.

The Dow fell 247 points or 3.1 percent to close at 7,695 on Friday as an earnings warning from consumer products giant Gillette sparked worries about U.S. earnings and a dollar drop accelerated the selloff.

But Australian market watchers do not expect a major slide on Monday morning, given the relatively subdued reaction by the Australian share futures market in New York trade and the local market's reluctance to believe in the Dow's earlier rally over 8,000.
The September share futures contract fell 49 points or 1.8 percent on Friday night.
As the Dow rose 5.8 percent in July and early August to its all-time high of 8,259 on August 6, the Australian market actually fell 1.1 percent.
To drive home the point, the Dow has fallen a total 6.8 percent from its August 6 high, but the Australian market has fallen only 2.2 percent.
Results from major local companies John Fairfax, Normandy Mining and others are seen driving sentiment later in the week.
Local bond and currency markets are seen opening steady, with the focus this week on the Reserve Bank of Australia's quarterly bulletin on Tuesday.
The Federal Reserve's Federal Open Markets Committee (FOMC) meeting later on Tuesday is seen the key overseas focus.
The FOMC is not expected to raise rates, but markets will be making sure when the meeting concludes early Wednesday morning local time.

The RBA bulletin is expected to repeat Governor Ian Macfarlane's sentiments from a speech last week -- that current monetary policy settings are not restricitve and the economy has substantial growth potential given the positive outlook for wages and inflation.

While a sixth interest rate cut is still seen as a less than even money bet, the odds have increased over the past two weeks. The median forecast of economists surveyed by Reuters showed a 40 percent chance of there being another rate cut, up from 30 percent two weeks ago.

If a cut does come, it will most likely be in the fourth quarter of the year, with the days after the November board meeting the most favoured time. By then the RBA will have another round of wage and inflation data to consider.
There were some who thought there was a good chance of a September rate cut if activity data over the next couple of weks remained soft.
One piece of data they may be able to use is enterprise bargaining wage agreements, which may be released by the Department of Industrial Relations this week.
The data is expected to show annual wages growth of around 4.5 percent, compared to the average weekly ordinary time earnings data released last Thursdya showing annual growth of juat 3.5 percent.

Other data out next week includes June quarter company profits, a component of GDP. Profits are expected to have risen by 2.3 percent in the quarter, implying a positive contribution to second quarter growth.
AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR

There is little on the horizon that is seen having the potential to propel the dollar out of the US$0.73/75 range it has traded since the beginning of July, with the FOMC not expected to lift rates and the impact of the RBA bulletin having been softened by Macfarlane's speech last week.

Traders said the solid gains through last week -- the dollar eose over a cent -- should see it try and test higher as long it manages to hold above US$0.7420. It closed in New York on Friday at US$0.7424/29.
Below there, US$0.7380 should prove solid, and it would take some very weak economic news that led to concerted talk of a near term rate cut to spark a test of US$0.7300.
On the crosses, ongoing weakness in regional Asian currencies was expected to remain a weight on the yen and a benefit to the Australian dollar.
AUSTRALIAN STOCKS
After an initial Dow-fuelled hiccup, the key factor for Australian stocks this week will be the ongoing annual results season.

"We have a lot of results coming up and the Federal Reserve meets on Tuesday. My best guess is that we'll probably be a little bit firmer, but not a lot," analyst David Perry of Austock Brokers said before the Dow's fall.
Some others were not as sanguine, suggesting that on a longer term outlook both U.S. and Australian markets were in a retracement phase with the day to day moves not an accurate indicator.
"I still believe that this market and the U.S. market is in some kind of a correction mode. It may not show every day though," said institutional desk head at one investment bank.
Some of the big results impressed last week, notably Lend Lease and Leighton Holdings, and the numbers due this week will be keenly watched for any surprises.
At this stage Tuesday and Wednesday see most of the action.
Tuesday sees John Fairfax Holdings Ltd report full year results, while fellow newspaper publisher Australian Provincial Newspapers announces half year numbers.
Capral Aluminium posts half year data, while gold miners North Flinders Mines Ltd and Mt Leyshon report full year numbers ahead of their major shareholder, Normandy Mining which reports on Wednesday.
The big one on Wednesday is Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation which has full year results.
Building materials firm Pioneer International also reports full year numbers on Wednesday, while its partner in petroleum Caltex Australia announces half year data.
Thursday has infrastructure investor Transurban reporting full year data, with labour agency Skilled Engineering also posting annual numbers.
AUSTRALIAN BONDS
The Australian bond market should start the week with a flat tone after U.S. Treasuries ended mixed on Friday in the wake of a bounce-back from initial selling.

With very little local data due this week, the U.S. is likely to be once again the main driving force for the market, although positive domestic fundamentals and hopes of a further easing in monetary policy could see the market outperform any U.S. move, analysts said.
This week's two key central bank set pieces both locally and in the U.S. have been somewhat watered down by actions in the past week and should prove non-events.

The Reserve Bank releases its quarterly bulletin on Tuesday, although the tone of it is expected to run on similar lines to comments by RBA governor last week where he was pushing growth but saw few inflationary presures.

Equally last week's barrage of data in the U.S. confirmed that inflation pressures were well under control, making it most unlikely that Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee will endorse a policy tightening.
Indeed Fed tightening expectations have now been pushed out to the FOMC meeting in November.

Domestic bonds succumbed to fairly choppy trading last week, largely due to a volatile U.S. Treasury market, which had taken local long dated yields to their highest level in nearly a month before rebounding on a weak set of wages data which is seen setting the ground work for another easing in monetary policy.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
